catalog_quote: Las raíces son monosílabas o bisílabas. Son los morfemas principales. Llevan un acento prosódico muy ligero al principio que se conserva siempre en su lugar de origen aunque estén acompañadas de prefijos. En las raíces monosílabas, además de llevar el acento prosódico, la vocal se alarga más o menos al doble aunque tenga un solo tono. ... En las frases pronunciadas, tanto por el acento prosódico como por la duración de las vocales, se puede identificar con exactitud cuales morfemas son raíces y cuales son determinantes. Por ejemplo, en las frases cu³ndú¹ voy a cardar y cu⁴ndú²¹ voy a montar, hay un contraste mínimo entre sus formas. La primera está acentuada en la penúltima sílaba y no tiene vocales largas. La segunda está acentuada en la última sílaba donde también tiene la vocal alargada. ... podemos concluir que -u³ndu¹ es la raíz o radical de la primera frase con c como determinante, y que ndu²¹ es la raíz de la segunda frase con cu⁴ como determinante. [p. 779, sec. 8 Raíces] ... Para el hablante nativo, tanto el acento prosódico como la duración de vocales son fáciles de predecir, y por tal motivo no las señalamos en la ortografía. [p. 777, sec. 5] ... [Los determinantes: prefijos de los verbos, pronombres inseparables y relativos, adjetivos demostrativos, algunos adverbios y algunas partículas] Son de una sílaba, sin acento prosódico, con una vocal corta como elemento central. [p. 778, sec. 7]

Llevan un acento prosódico muy ligero al principio que se conserva siempre en su lugar de origen aunque estén acompañadas de prefijos. [p. 779] … En las raíces bisílabas, la vocal de la primera sílaba, la que lleva el acento prosódico, no se alarga excepto cuando el ambiente sintáctico provoca un deslizamiento de su tono. new_statements.translation: Roots are monosyllabic or disyllabic. They are the principal morphemes. They carry a very light prosodic accent at their beginning, which is always kept in its original place even when they are accompanied by prefixes. [p. 779] … In disyllabic roots, the vowel of the first syllable, the one that bears the prosodic accent, is not lengthened except when the syntactic environment causes its tone to glide. For the native speaker both the prosodic accent and vowel length are easy to predict, and for that reason we do not mark them in the orthography. [p. 777] … [Determinants — verb prefixes, bound and relative pronouns, demonstratives, some adverbs and particles —] are monosyllabic, without prosodic accent, with a short vowel as their nucleus. [p. 778]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (a 'very light' prosodic accent) is non-contrastive and predictable: it falls on the first syllable of the root, and roots are one or two syllables long; the monosyllabic prefixes/proclitic 'determinants' never carry it, so the accent stays on the root when prefixes are added. Word position therefore follows root position, not an edge count: cu3ndu1 'I am going to card' (root -u3ndu1) is accented on the penult, cu4ndu21 'I am going to mount' (root ndu21) on the final syllable, whose vowel is also lengthened (monosyllabic roots lengthen their vowel about twofold). Needham & Davis 1946: 140 (Concepción Pápalo) concur: stress is not phonemic and 'appears to fall on the first syllable of most morphemes'.
new_statements.exceptions: Needham & Davis 1946: 140 hedge that placement conditions were 'still not too clear' and allow 'possible placement on a high tone at the end of a morpheme'. Anderson & Concepción 1983: 784-785 (sec. 18): Spanish loanwords keep their Spanish stress position, which is mapped onto fixed tone melodies (e.g. accent on penult -> tones 2-4 on penult-final); an orthographic accent is otherwise used only to mark the 1sg tone-1 morpheme (sec. 20, p. 787).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root plus prefixed determinants), described for citation/dictionary forms and short verb phrases; both sources treat the language as tonal (1983: four levels for Santa María Pápalo; 1946: three registers for Concepción Pápalo) with stress non-phonemic. The deciding source is the phonology appendix of a dictionary (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a phonology), not a stand-alone grammar.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Anderson & Concepción Roque 1983) is based on data collected in Santa María Pápalo (p. vii), which Glottolog lists as the dialect sant1437 under tepe1280; Needham & Davis 1946 and Davis & Walker 1955 describe the Concepción Pápalo dialect (no separate glottocode; Glottolog files Bradley's 'Concepción Pápalo Cuicatec' sketch under tepe1280). Both are ISO cux; the variety of San Juan Tepeuxila itself is only described in Davis & Bravo n.d. (not seen). The two dialect descriptions agree on root-initial, non-phonemic stress but differ on tone inventory (four levels vs three registers).

new_statements.quote: A third feature which varies from the transcription in the source materials is vowel length. Stress and vowel length are easily predictable. Roots are either bisyllabic or monosyllabic, and stress occurs on the first syllable. Vowel length is a concomitant of stress and hence does not need to be represented in the orthography (Anderson and Concepción R. 1983:777). [p. 417] … There are three tones: high (written with acute accent), mid (written with macron), and low (unmarked). Cuicatec exhibits tone sandhi in which the basic tone of words in isolation is changed in the context of the tones on certain other words (Longacre 1957:96-100). [p. 416]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Anderson & Concepción 1983 statement (root-initial stress, which the dictionary says is kept in place under prefixation) and it fills the catalog record's empty rule; adds that vowel length is a concomitant of stress and that the language has three surface tones with sandhi (collapsed from the dictionary's four). Describes the Concepción Pápalo town dialect rather than the catalog's Santa María Pápalo, but Bradley cites Egland 1978:9 for 98% intelligibility between the two and takes the stress rule from the Santa María Pápalo dictionary itself.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable: roots are one or two syllables and stress falls on the first syllable of the root; vowel length is a by-product of stress (stressed vowel long) and is therefore not. Tone (three surface tones, with sandhi) is a separate system from stress. Bradley takes the stress rule from the Santa María Pápalo dictionary (Anderson & Concepción R. 1983:777), whose fuller statement says the root-initial accent stays on the root when prefixes are added, so 'first syllable' here is the first syllable of the root, not necessarily of the word.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions stated. Bradley notes that inconsistencies in laryngealized vowels in the source texts may reflect 'laryngealization loss in unstressed syllables' (p. 417), and that a doubled vowel in his transcription marks a tone sequence on one syllable, not vowel length (pp. 417-418). The stress statement is second-hand: Bradley worked from published texts with no native speaker available (p. 416) and cites the dictionary for stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Bradley 1991 describes the Concepción Pápalo dialect (data: four published folklore texts by Marjorie Davis 1954, 1962, supplemented by Needham & Davis 1946, Davis & Walker 1955, Longacre 1957 and the Santa María Pápalo dictionary). SIL files it under language code cux (Tepeuxila Cuicatec), the same ISO language as the catalog item tepe1280, whose only Glottolog dialect is Santa María Pápalo (sant1437). Bradley reports 98% intelligibility between the two towns (Egland 1978:9) and his stress rule is taken from the Santa María Pápalo dictionary, so the statement applies to the catalog's variety.
